projects.title: NYC Language Explorer
projects.description: Free interactive tool from the Department of City Planning, launched July 2026, presenting tables, maps and charts on the languages spoken by New Yorkers with limited English proficiency, drawn from Census American Community Survey data. Users can start from a neighborhood or borough to see the most common languages, or pick a language to see where its speakers concentrate across the five boroughs. Roughly 1.8 million New Yorkers have limited English proficiency; Spanish leads in every borough except Staten Island, where Chinese ranks first.
projects.why_interesting: Built to help agencies meet Local Law 30 language-access mandates, it turns a compliance obligation into a public-facing map of the city's linguistic geography -- a durable reference for anyone reporting on immigration, services or neighborhood change.

projects.title: 311 Tracker
projects.description: Searchable database letting New Yorkers look up any residential building's 311 complaints, housing violations, eviction history and rent-stabilization status, covering roughly 834,400 buildings and 2.0 million Department of Housing Preservation and Development violations. Featured in BetaNYC's July 16 civic-tech roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Consolidates several of the city's clunkiest housing datasets into one address lookup -- the kind of tenant-facing tool that reframes open data as consumer protection, echoing Apartment Audit NYC from the July 3 scan.

projects.title: Close
projects.description: Map that colors every block by how far it sits from its most distant essential amenity -- grocery, pharmacy, school, park and the like -- surfacing which neighborhoods are genuinely walkable to daily needs and which are amenity deserts. Highlighted in BetaNYC's July 16 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: A rigorous, block-level take on the 15-minute-city idea that inverts the usual proximity map: instead of shading what is close, it shades what is worst-served, making gaps in access legible.

projects.title: NYC Sim
projects.description: Browser-based simulator that lets anyone explore interactive 3D models of Manhattan, featured in BetaNYC's July 16 civic-tech roundup.
projects.why_interesting: A lightweight, no-install path into a Manhattan digital twin at a moment when the city's official digital-twin project is still years from public release -- civic 3D modeling that runs in a tab.

projects.title: TicketTriage NYC
projects.description: Tool that transforms NYC's raw parking-ticket data into readable tables and summaries, letting users see where and how the city writes violations. Surfaced in BetaNYC's July 16 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Parking enforcement is one of the city's most regressive and least-examined revenue streams; making the ticket data browsable opens a rarely-scrutinized fiscal and equity story.

projects.title: Metropolitan Diary Map
projects.description: Austin Steinhart's map plotting 50 years of New York Times Metropolitan Diary columns to the street locations of the small-moment stories they describe. Featured in BetaNYC's July 16 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: A rare geography of the city's emotional and anecdotal life rather than its infrastructure -- half a century of overheard New York moments turned into a browsable map.

projects.title: New York Times: American ancestry map
projects.description: Upshot interactive by Albert Sun, Jeff Adelson and Larry Buchanan (published July 2026) coloring every U.S. census tract by the mix of ancestries its residents report, blending nearly 200 distinct identities so that neighborhoods where several groups live side by side take on mixed hues. Announced via the Upshot's official account.
projects.why_interesting: A national tract-level map that resists tidy category boundaries, rendering the overlap and blending of American identity as color rather than hard lines -- an unusually literary approach to demographic cartography.

projects.title: Beacon
projects.description: DataKind-built platform that combines public data on economic security, health and housing with organizations' own data to generate place-based maps for community groups. Featured in BetaNYC's July 9 civic-tech roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Aimed squarely at nonprofits that lack in-house data teams, it lowers the barrier to place-based analysis -- a reusable civic-data layer rather than a single one-off dashboard.

projects.title: ForkMesh
projects.description: Local-first source-code preservation and collaboration infrastructure aimed at civic-tech and open-source projects, surfaced in BetaNYC's July 9 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Civic-tech tools are notoriously fragile -- they vanish when a maintainer moves on or a host shuts down. This tackles the durability problem directly, treating preservation as core infrastructure.

projects.title: New York State Regulatory Reset
projects.description: State initiative, built with Recoding America and Stanford University, that used AI to analyze roughly 18 million words of New York State law, flagging outdated requirements -- fee schedules, notary rules and the like -- for agencies to eliminate or modernize. Reported in BetaNYC's July 9 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: One of the first large-scale government uses of AI to audit its own legal code for obsolescence -- a concrete test of whether machine analysis can meaningfully speed regulatory cleanup.

projects.title: BetaNYC New York City Budget (Schedule C discretionary awards)
projects.description: Open repository containing twenty years of NYC Council Schedule C discretionary awards (FY2009-FY2027) in structured, queryable form -- scraped from PDFs and reconciled by an AI agent. Announced in BetaNYC's July 9 roundup.
projects.why_interesting: Council discretionary funding has always been locked in annual PDFs; a two-decade machine-readable ledger makes it possible to trace member spending patterns and follow the money over time.

projects.title: BetaNYC civic AI / MCP connectors
projects.description: Free, open-source Model Context Protocol connectors giving AI assistants direct access to NYC Council legislation, city spending and contracts, 311 service data, the City Record, the NYC Charter and Administrative Code, and NYS Open Legislation. The nyc-council-mcp connector shipped a v2.2.0 fix that had been hiding thousands of Council resolutions from search. Featured across BetaNYC's July 9 and 16 roundups.
projects.why_interesting: Plumbing that lets any AI tool query core NYC civic datasets directly -- the connective layer that could make the next wave of civic-tech tools far faster to build.
